extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and novelists interested in Henry James's theory of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria for composing and evaluating the literary novel according to Henry James's Art of Fiction: principles about purpose, form, character, morality, and execution that guide literary realism and artistic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel's primary responsibility: represent life
rubrics_metrics.description: "At the core of James’s definition of the novel is what he sees as its responsibility to represent life. He states that this is 'the only reason for the existence of a novel' (1884: 46)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation of life should be central to the novel's purpose. This representation is not a simple photographic copy but a personal, direct impression of life refracted through the novelist’s imagination and observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: A novel ought to be artistic (craft + genius)
rubrics_metrics.description: James treats 'art' as combining proficiency in craft (from apprenticeship) and the individual creative genius celebrated by Romantic writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good fiction must show technical skill as well as imaginative originality: both practiced workmanship and an intense individual sensibility are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air of reality rather than crude realism
rubrics_metrics.description: James values more the 'air of reality' than crude photographic realism, distancing the novel from mere realism associated with photography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novel should create a convincing atmosphere of reality through imaginative shaping, not by slavishly reproducing outward facts; aim for the impression of life rather than literal accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative power: 'guess the unseen from the seen'
rubrics_metrics.description: "The power to guess the unseen from the seen, to trace the implication of things, to judge the whole piece by the pattern' (1884: 53)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should infer and suggest underlying realities and relations rather than stating everything explicitly; patterning and implication are markers of artistic perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic unity: the novel as a living, continuous thing
rubrics_metrics.description: "A novel is a living thing, all one and continuous, like any other organism..." (1884: 54).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The parts of the novel (plot, character, dialogue, description, narration) should interpenetrate; unity and continuity across the work are signs of vitality. Avoid fragmented, disjointed composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid writing in 'blocks' and obtrusive authorial voice
rubrics_metrics.description: James condemns composition 'existing in a series of blocks' and novels where the author's or narrator's voice is obtrusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let sections feel isolated or let authorial intrusions break the novel's organic flow. Avoid overt authorial commentary and obvious author-text biographical alignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-driven development: plot should issue from characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are 'analogous to the seeds of a plant': the novel should develop outwardly from the nature of those characters, the plot resulting from their characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let characters' internal nature and decisions generate events; avoid imposing plot mechanics that are disconnected from character psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for form from within the subject ('logic of the particular case')
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'search for form' is central: the most effective structure and narration are discovered from within the subject itself, not by imposing existing patterns or sterile rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form should emerge organically out of the material; resist formulaic structures and preconceived templates. Use the subject's internal demands to determine shape and method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject externally imposed 'conscious moral purpose'
rubrics_metrics.description: James repudiates the notion that the novel must be governed by a pre-stated 'conscious moral purpose' or conventional moulds (Besant's view).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write to demonstrate a predetermined moral lesson; moral effect should arise naturally from the work's intelligence and sensibility rather than propaganda or sermonizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only obligation in advance: be interesting
rubrics_metrics.description: James: 'the only obligation to which in advance we may hold a novel ... is that it be interesting' (1884: 49).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize sustaining interest; novelty of subject, depth of handling, and imaginative presentation are ways to fulfill this obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of execution: judge how the subject is treated
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality is estimated by applying 'the test of execution' — what an author has done with his or her subject (1884: 50).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the novel on its realized treatment of its chosen subject: coherence, development, and responsiveness to the subject determine success; excess detail or distraction can fail the test (example: critique of Middlemarch as 'treasure-house of details' but an 'indifferent whole').

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and artistic senses converge in depth of the producer's mind
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is one point at which the moral sense and the artistic sense lie very near together... No good novel will ever proceed from a superficial mind.' (1884: 63–4)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The moral value of a novel depends on the depth and felt life of the creator's sensibility; intelligence and moral consciousness are linked and reflected in artistic subtlety rather than explicit moralizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey the whole field of experience; include morally complex material
rubrics_metrics.description: James argues the 'essence of moral energy is to survey the whole field' and novelists should not limit representation to the morally exemplary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray a wide range of human experience, including morally ambiguous and non-exemplary aspects, to foster 'stirred intelligence' and critical reflection in readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel's scope and power: extend experience and develop reader's intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel is 'the great extension, great beyond all others, of experience and of consciousness' (1907–9: 1061); it can 'renovate and develop the mind' by engaging readers in form, content, and subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for experiments of scope and consciousness that challenge and expand reader understanding; the novel's artistic ambition is measured by its capacity to deepen perception and moral sensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial ownership of subject and retrospective appreciation of form
rubrics_metrics.description: The author should be granted his 'subject' and 'the form of which is to be appreciated after the fact' (1884: 56, 50). If the reader dislikes the subject, the novel can be abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow the subject to guide composition; formal coherence may only be apparent after the work's completion. Authors should pursue their chosen subject confidently rather than tailoring to immediate reader preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conventional, traditional moulds and clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: James warns against confining the subject to 'conventional, traditional moulds' which reduce it to 'an eternal repetition of a few familiar clichés' (1884: 58).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of stock plots, facile moralizing, or trite resolutions; seek fresh treatment and particularity instead of formulaic repetition.
